strengths: Addresses a genuine gap in code-generation evaluation: existing benchmarks mostly test single-turn or self-invoking code generation, not the iterative, dependency-aware 'codeflow' process where developers build up complex solutions by reusing previously implemented functions across turns.

The automated data curation pipeline is well described and technically substantial, sourcing from Codeforces editorials (rather than scraped user solutions) to avoid ethical/quality concerns, and enabling continuous, contamination-resistant updates.

Good scale and diversity (5,258 problems) with an AST-derived dependency structure that yields useful auxiliary labels (overall-turns, overall-depth) which correlate well with the established Codeforces difficulty rating, lending some validation to the automatic labeling.
Proposes new metrics (Pass Depth/APD, DSC) that go beyond simple pass@k to give finer-grained diagnostic information about where/why models fail in multi-turn chains.

Broad and relevant experimental coverage across many closed- and open-source LLMs (reasoning models, coder-specialized models, general models across parameter scales), producing a consistent and interesting empirical finding: substantial performance drop from single-turn to multi-turn, and rapid degradation with more turns/depth/complex dependency structure (DSC).

The manual error taxonomy (Incomplete Reasoning, Insufficient Globalization, Instruction Misinterpretation) with concrete case studies gives useful qualitative insight into why multi-turn code reuse is hard for current models, beyond aggregate scores.
weaknesses: Substantial parts of the benchmark construction itself rely on LLMs (Deepseek-R1 for solution regeneration, Deepseek-V3 for subproblem statement generation and function selection) with no reported human verification of the quality, correctness, or naturalness of the resulting subproblem descriptions/decompositions; benchmark quality issues (ambiguous or ill-posed subproblem statements) could confound the reported model failures with dataset noise.

The 'codeflow' decomposition is derived post-hoc from monolithic competitive-programming solutions rewritten into functions by an LLM, which may produce artificial modularizations that do not necessarily reflect how real developers organize code, weakening the ecological validity of the 'real-world development' framing despite this being the paper's core motivation.

Test cases for intermediate subproblems are generated purely by capturing I/O from executing one generated reference solution on the public sample tests, so subproblem-level unit tests may have very limited input coverage (few edge cases) and could pass with incorrect logic that happens to match the recorded trace, raising reliability/soundness concerns for the pass@k and PD numbers.

The manual error-annotation study (Table 2/3) underlying the taxonomy and IR-remediation-rate analysis is based on an unspecified, apparently small sample and only two models, limiting the generalizability and statistical confidence of the qualitative error analysis conclusions.

Comparisons between single-turn and multi-turn settings may not be fully apples-to-apples: the multi-turn setting requires stepwise reuse and context carry-over while the single-turn setting exposes the model to the full set of functions and background at once, so part of the observed gap could reflect differences in task framing/information exposure rather than purely 'multi-turn ability' as claimed.

Reproducibility is weakened by dependence on multiple LLM-driven pipeline stages (which are stochastic and dependent on specific proprietary/open models that may change over time), and by the fact that code and dataset are stated as 'to be released soon' rather than available at submission.

The writing has noticeable grammatical errors and awkward phrasing throughout, and some methodological details (e.g., exact sample sizes for pass@k, number of trials k, exact test-set construction/held-out selection criteria beyond 'most recent 20%') are underspecified, which could hamper precise replication.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and under-explored gap in code-generation benchmarking: multi-turn, dependency-aware 'codeflow' generation that mirrors realistic modular software development, as opposed to single-shot function synthesis captured by HumanEval/MBPP-style benchmarks.

The automated data-curation pipeline (scraping problems + official editorials, LLM-assisted solution normalization verified via actual Codeforces submission, AST-based dependency decomposition, and I/O-capture based subproblem test generation) is well documented in the appendix and designed for continuous, low-contamination refresh, which is valuable for benchmark longevity.

Introduces two thoughtful new metrics (Pass Depth/Average Pass Depth and Dependency Structure Complexity) that go beyond coarse pass@k to give fine-grained, structure-aware diagnostics of where and how models fail in multi-turn chains.

Broad and reasonably systematic empirical study spanning 14 closed- and open-source models (including reasoning models), consistently showing a large multi-turn vs. single-turn performance gap and structural-complexity sensitivity, which is a useful and non-obvious empirical finding for the community.

The error taxonomy (Incomplete Reasoning / Insufficient Globalization / Instruction Misinterpretation) plus the IR-remediation-rate analysis offers an interpretable account of why multi-turn code reuse is hard, going beyond aggregate scores to actionable failure modes.
weaknesses: Substantial parts of the benchmark's ground truth are LLM-generated (solution normalization via DeepSeek-R1, subproblem statements/dependencies via DeepSeek-V3) with only the top-level solution verified by Codeforces submission; the quality/correctness of the LLM-authored subproblem descriptions and the fidelity of the induced dependency decomposition are not independently validated (no reported human audit rate, agreement statistics, or error rate for this stage), which is a soundness/reproducibility concern for a benchmark whose main claim is quality and reliability.

Subproblem unit tests are captured purely from executions of one reference implementation's I/O at each call site; this only checks conformity to one specific (and somewhat arbitrary) decomposition/signature choice and does not establish edge-case coverage, so correct-but-differently-structured model solutions could be unfairly penalized (false negatives), and this risk is not discussed or quantified.

The manual error-annotation study underlying Tables 2–3 (IR/IG/IM proportions, IR remediation rate) reports no sample size, annotator count, or inter-annotator agreement, making it hard to judge the reliability of these fairly strong qualitative conclusions.

Key experimental protocol details (number of samples per problem for pass@k, temperature/decoding settings, k values, cost/compute budget) are deferred entirely to an appendix not shown/fully specified in the main text, limiting the reader's ability to judge robustness of the reported numbers from the manuscript alone.

The paper states code/data 'will be available soon' rather than providing it, which weakens the reproducibility guarantee at review time for a paper whose central contribution is the released benchmark and pipeline.

Comparisons to closely related prior multi-turn/iterative benchmarks (MTPB, CodeEvalPro, InterCode) are qualitative assertions of insufficient difficulty rather than direct empirical comparisons, so the incremental positioning relative to existing multi-turn benchmarks is not rigorously substantiated.

No human performance baseline or independent difficulty calibration for the codeflow-decomposed task itself (as opposed to citing general Codeforces pass-rate difficulty) is provided, so the claimed 'high difficulty' of the benchmark's multi-turn formulation specifically is partly asserted rather than demonstrated.
Minor writing/polish issues (e.g., an apparently truncated sentence at the end of the abstract, some redundant/awkward phrasing) suggest the manuscript could benefit from another editing pass.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and underexplored gap in code generation evaluation: multi-turn, dependency-aware 'codeflow' generation that mirrors modular software engineering practice, distinct from single-turn benchmarks (HumanEval, MBPP) and bug-fix-oriented benchmarks (SWE-Bench).

The automated data curation pipeline (AST-based dependency extraction, topological subproblem decomposition, instrumented test-case harvesting) is well-engineered, general, and appears reasonably reproducible given the detailed appendix (prompt templates, cost estimates, sampling protocols).

The authors conduct non-trivial ablation studies to check for LLM-induced bias in the pipeline (cross-model description consistency, structural stability of decomposition across different backbone LLMs, human-LLM quality cross-validation), which strengthens confidence in the pipeline's soundness.

Large-scale empirical evaluation across 19 models (closed- and open-source, various scales) with consistent multi-turn vs single-turn comparisons, yielding clear and interpretable findings (substantial performance degradation in multi-turn settings, inverse correlation between dependency complexity and performance).
Introduction of principled structural metrics (APD, APT, DSC) with a formally derived unbiased estimator, going beyond simple Pass@k to capture partial progress and depth-wise failure patterns.
Correlation of structural complexity metrics with official Codeforces difficulty ratings provides external validation that the decomposition captures meaningful task difficulty.
Fine-grained qualitative error taxonomy (Incomplete Reasoning, Insufficient Globalization, Instruction Misinterpretation) with concrete case studies adds interpretive value beyond aggregate scores.
weaknesses: CodeFlowBench-Repo, despite being marketed as the 'real-world' component, ends up quite small after filtering (only 70 multi-turn problems augmented with 60 single-turn problems across five domains), raising concerns about statistical robustness and generalizability of Repo-specific conclusions (e.g., domain-wise error distributions, depth-4 APD values in Table 1 which are based on very few samples).

The single-turn baseline is constructed by providing the model with all subproblem descriptions and dependency structure simultaneously and asking for one-shot generation of all functions; this differs from a 'naive' single-turn setting (i.e., only the top-level problem statement) and could partly confound the reported multi-turn vs single-turn gap, since the single-turn condition still benefits from the same decomposition scaffolding.

Quality control of LLM-generated content (subproblem statements, solution decomposition, editorial-to-code conversion) relies substantially on other LLMs and limited human spot-checking; the validation rubric explicitly instructs graders 'not to be overly strict' and to never score below 2/5, which could mask systematic description quality issues and creates some circularity (using LLMs to judge LLM-generated artifacts).

Manual error-type annotation in Table 3 is performed only by the authors on a sampled subset, with no inter-annotator agreement or sample size reported, limiting confidence in the fine-grained error analysis.

Some central claims (e.g., 'dependency complexity inversely correlates with performance', degraded multi-turn performance) are intuitively expected outcomes; the paper's main novel contribution is the benchmark/pipeline and metrics rather than a surprising empirical finding.

The paper is very densely packed, deferring most methodological and reproducibility details (prompts, sampling protocol, k for Pass@k, test environment specifics) to a lengthy appendix, which somewhat obscures core methodological choices in the main text and complicates independent verification without the appendix.

strengths: The paper identifies a genuine and underexplored gap in code-generation evaluation: existing benchmarks (HumanEval, MBPP, SWE-Bench, MTPB) either test single-turn generation or lack paired unit tests and sufficient dependency complexity for multi-turn, modular code reuse. The codeflow formalization is a clear and well-motivated contribution.

The data curation pipeline is thoughtfully engineered: it scrapes problems/editorials, converts them to verified solutions via live judge submission, and automatically decomposes solutions into dependency-ordered subproblems with instrumented I/O capture for unit tests. This is a genuinely reusable and extensible framework, and the appendix documents it in unusual depth (prompts, anchor-matching heuristics, cost estimates).

Two complementary datasets (algorithmic Comp and real-world Repo) broaden the evaluative scope, and the correlation of structural metrics (turns, depth) with official Codeforces ratings provides external validation that the difficulty labels are meaningful, not arbitrary.

The proposed diagnostic metrics (APD, APT, DSC) go beyond simple Pass@k and offer a principled way to localize failure depth, which is used effectively to produce non-trivial findings (e.g., reasoning models excel at shallow depth but fail to scale to deep dependencies; error-type shifts from IM to IR as model quality increases).

Reasonably thorough robustness checks for pipeline bias: cross-model comparison of descriptions (ROUGE/BERT similarity), structural stability of decomposition across LLMs, and human-LLM cross-validation of subproblem quality.

Broad experimental coverage (19 models spanning closed/open-source, various scales) with consistent, interpretable trends (large multi-turn vs single-turn gaps, capacity vs. reasoning trade-offs at different depths), supported by manually annotated error-type case studies that add qualitative insight beyond aggregate numbers.
Sampling procedure for CodeFlowBench-Comp test subset is statistically validated (stratified sampling + chi-square test), which is a nice touch for reproducibility rigor.
weaknesses: CodeFlowBench-Repo is very small after filtering (only 70 multi-turn problems survived from 749 candidates, augmented with 60 single-turn problems), and the Computation domain was dropped entirely due to empty dependency trees—this undercuts the claim of comprehensively capturing 'real-world' diversity and raises concerns about statistical robustness of Repo-based conclusions.

Canonical solutions and subproblem descriptions for CodeFlowBench-Comp are both LLM-generated (DeepSeek-R1 for code, DeepSeek-V3 for descriptions) rather than sourced from genuine human decompositions; although verified for functional correctness via the online judge, the decomposition granularity/style itself is an LLM artifact, which could bias which failure modes are observed (e.g., whether subproblem boundaries are 'natural').

The manual error-type annotation (IR/IG/IM) is performed solely by the authors on a sampled subset, with no inter-annotator agreement statistics reported, limiting confidence in the fine-grained error analysis as an objective/reproducible measurement.

It is unclear how many trials (n) underlie the reported Pass@1/APD@1 numbers in the main table; no variance or confidence intervals are given for the central results, making it hard to assess how much of the observed model ranking differences (e.g., GPT-5 vs Gemini-3) are statistically meaningful versus sampling noise.

The task setup always supplies the full overarching problem background B at every turn in addition to prior code, which is a design choice that may not fully mirror realistic incremental development (where full future context is not always available), and this simplification isn't discussed as a limitation.

The relationship to closely related prior multi-step/self-invoking benchmarks (e.g., HumanEval Pro/MBPP Pro, InterCode) is only briefly discussed; a more detailed differentiation of what genuinely new failure modes CodeFlowBench captures beyond these would strengthen the novelty claim.

Given the benchmark's reliance on recent proprietary models and competitive-programming/GitHub sources tied to specific dates, the benchmark's 'update mechanism' for avoiding contamination is asserted but not empirically demonstrated (e.g., no contamination analysis is shown for the newest problems used).
